rules.rationale: Dense heteroatoms provide hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors and dipoles that strongly stabilize the aqueous phase.
Pure hydrocarbons offer only dispersion contacts, so cavity formation cost dominates hydration free energy.
Source evidence favors short SMILES; small solutes pay low cavity cost with polar groups fully solvent exposed.
Heavy halogenation adds hydrophobic, weakly polar surface that degrades hydration despite nominal heteroatom count.

skill.hypothesis: Transfers polarity-driven hydration plus the source short-SMILES prior, now separating halogen hydrophobicity from heteroatom polarity. May fail if intramolecular hydrogen bonding shields polar groups.

rules.rationale: Counter to the source ring effect: acyclic chains expose donors flexibly, but transfer is weak so weight is small.
Flat aromatic surfaces hydrate poorly; pi systems give weak, entropically costly water ordering.
Moderate heteroatom content balances hydrogen bonding against added hydrophobic scaffold, a common hydration optimum.
Heavy branching sterically buries polar sites, reducing effective solvent-accessible hydrogen-bonding area.

skill.hypothesis: Downweights the uncertain source ring relation and bets that aromatic surface area, not ring count, governs hydration. Fails if polar heterocycles dominate the top candidates.
